Title: Observer Pattern and B-Trees: Design and Data Structure Essentials

Observer pattern:
- Definition: behavioral design pattern, subject maintains list of observers, notifies state changes.
- Components: Subject, Observer interface, ConcreteSubject, ConcreteObserver. Subject has attach/detach/notify. Observer has update. Subject state changes call notify, observers update.
- Push vs pull: subject sends data or observer pulls.
- Complexity: attach/detach O(1) if list append/remove? Actually remove from list O(n) if array; if using linked list with references O(1). Notification O(k) where k observers. Space O(k). If observer update expensive, not counted. Need mention.
- Benefits: open/closed, decoupling, broadcast, dynamic subscription. Drawbacks: memory leaks if not detached, unexpected updates, order issues, complexity.
- Alternatives: event bus, pub/sub, signals/slots, reactive streams, polling. Choose when multiple objects need react to changes without subject knowing them; when event-driven UI; when need dynamic. Avoid when simple one-to-one, tight coupling, performance critical with many observers, or need guaranteed order? Actually can use callbacks.
- Examples: Java Swing/AWT event listeners; DOM addEventListener; JavaBeans PropertyChangeListener; Android LiveData/Flow? Observer pattern; RxJS Observables; Model-View-Controller; distributed pub/sub (Redis, Kafka) but more than observer.

B-trees:
- Definition: self-balancing tree, multi-way, sorted, all leaves same depth. Node contains keys and child pointers. Order m: max m children, max m-1 keys; internal nodes at least ceil(m/2) children except root. Search: start root, compare keys, descend. Insert: find leaf, insert, split if overflow, propagate. Delete: borrow/merge if underflow.
- Complexity: height O(log_m n), operations O(log n) (base m but log n). Space O(n). Disk I/O: height small, each node page, so O(log_m n) disk accesses. For m=100, n=1e9, height ~5. Good.
- Variants: B+tree: data only in leaves, linked leaves for range scans; B* tree; B-tree vs B+.
- Alternatives: binary search tree, AVL, red-black, skip list, hash table, LSM tree. Choose B-tree when data on disk, need range queries, sorted order, high fanout, stable performance. Avoid for in-memory small data? AVL/red-black simpler; hash for point lookups; LSM for write-heavy.
- Examples: database indexes (MySQL InnoDB uses B+tree; PostgreSQL uses B-tree for indexes; SQLite uses B-tree), filesystems (ext4 directory htree, NTFS? NTFS uses B+tree for directory indexes?
